technical-data.invention-title: SYSTEM AND METHOD FOR PROTECTING DATA AND CORRECTING BIT ERRORS DUE TO COMPONENT FAILURES
SYSTEME ET PROCEDE POUR LA PROTECTION DE DONNEES ET LA CORRECTION D'ERREURS SUR BITS DUES AUX DEFAILLANCES DE COMPOSANTS

nplcit.text: "32-BIT-WIDE MEMORY TOLERATES FAILURES " NTIS TECH NOTES,US,US DEPARTMENT OF COMMERCE., October 1990 (1990-10), page 818 XP000171434 SPRINGFIELD, VA

abstract.p: A system for protecting data and correcting bit errors due to component failures. A check bits generation unit partitions the data into a plurality of logical groups. The check bits generation unit generates a parity bit for each of the logical groups, and additionally generates a global error correction. The global error correction code is equivalent to the result of generating individual error correction codes for each logical group and combining them in a predetermined manner. In one particular embodiment, the data is divided into a total of X logical groups. An error correction unit is coupled to receive the plurality of data bits and the check bits following storage or transmission. It is configured to generate a parity error bit for each of the logical groups of data based on the received data bits, and to generate a regenerated global error correction code in the same manner in which the original global error correction code is derived. A global syndrome code is generated such that, with knowledge of the specific logical groups that have a single bit error, a value indicative of the location of the error in such groups may be derived from the global syndrome code.

La présente invention concerne un système de protection de données et de correction d'erreurs sur bits dues aux défaillances de composants. Une unité de génération de bits de contrôle divise les données en une pluralité de groupes logiques. L'unité de génération de bits de contrôle génère une bit de parité pour chacun des groupes logiques, et génère en outre une correction d'erreurs globale. Le code de correction d'erreurs globale est équivalent au résultat de la génération de codes de correction d'erreurs individuelle pour chaque groupe logique et de leur combinaison d'une manière prédéterminée. Dans un mode de réalisation particulier, les données sont divisées en X groupes logiques au total. Une unité de correction est reliée pour recevoir la pluralité de bits de données et de bits de contrôle suite à la mise en mémoire ou à la transmission. Elle est présente une configuration permettant de générer un bit de contrôle pour chacun des groupes logiques de données basés sur les bits de données reçues, et de générer un code de correction globale de la même manière par laquelle le code de correction globale d'origine a été obtenue. Un code de syndrome global est généré de sorte que, en connaissant les groupes logiques spécifiques qui présentent un seule erreur sur bits, une valeur indicative de la location de l'erreur dans de tels groupes peut être déterminée à partir du code de syndrome global.

description.p: TITLE: SYSTEM AND METHOD FOR PROTECTING DATA AND CORRECTING BIT ERRORS DUE TO COMPONENT FAILURES
BACKGROUND OF THE INVENTION
1 Field of the Invention

This invention relates to error correction in electronic systems and, more particularly, to systems that employ error correction codes to facilitate correction of bit errors due to, for example, component failures
2. Description of the Related Art

Error codes are commonly used in electronic systems to detect and correct data errors, such as transmission errors or storage errors. For example, error codes may be used to detect and correct errors in data transmitted via a telephone line, a radio transmitter, or a compact disc laser. Error codes may additionally be used to detect and correct errors associated with data stored in the memory of computer systems. One common use of error codes is to detect and correct errors of data transmitted on a data bus of a computer system In such systems, error correction bits, or check bits, may be generated for the data prior to its transfer or storage When the data is received or retrieved, the check bits may be used to detect and correct errors withm the data.

Component failures are a common source of error in electrical systems. Faulty components may include faulty memory chips or faulty data paths provided between devices of a system. Faulty data paths can result from, for example, faulty pms, faulty data traces, or faulty wires.

Hamming codes are a commonly used type of error code. The check bits in a Hamming code are parity bits for portions of the data bits. Each check bit provides the parity for a unique subset of the data bits. If an error occurs (i.e. one or more of the data bits change state), one or more of the check bits upon regeneration will also change state (assuming the error is within the class of errors covered by the code). By determming the specific bits of the regenerated check bits that changed state, the location of the error within the data may be determined For example, if one data bit changes state, this data bit will cause one or more of the regenerated check bits to change state. Because each data bit contributes to a unique group of check bits, the check bits that are modified will identify the data bit that changed state. The error may be corrected by inverting the bit identified as being erroneous.

One common use of Hamming codes is to correct single bit errors within a group of data Generally speakmg, the number of check bits must be large enough such that 2k-l is greater than or equal to n+k where k is the number of check bits and n is the number of data bits Accordingly, seven check bits are typically required to implement a smgle error correcting Hamming code for 64 data bits A single error correcting Hamming code is capable of detecting and correcting a single error

Figures 1-3 illustrate an example of a system employing a single-error correction (SEC) Hamming code In this example, four data bits (D4, D3, D2, and Dl) are protected usmg three check bits (PI, P2, and P3) The parity generator 10 (Figure 1) is used to encode the data block that contains the data bits and the check bits The encodmg process is performed prior to stoπng or communicating the data. Figure 2 shows an assignment of data bits to calculate the check bits. In this example, the check bit PI is generated by an XOR
(exclusive OR) of the binary values m D4, D3, and Dl. Similarly, the check bit P2 is generated by an XOR of the binary values m D4, D2, and Dl, and the check bit P3 is generated by an XOR of the binary values in D3, D2 and Dl. Figure 3 shows the bit positions and the corresponding content of these positions withm the encoded data block. The data block, which includes the data bits and the generated check bits, may then be stored in a memory chip or communicated over a data communication path.

At the point of receipt, the data block is retrieved and decoded. The decoding process involves performing a validity check on the received word, and executing an error correction technique if an error was detected. To check whether an error occurred in the storage (or transmission) of the data block, the check bits PI, P2, and P3 are effectively regenerated using the received data, and each regenerated check bit is XORed with the corresponding received check bit to generate a corresponding syndrome bit. Figure 4 is a table depicting a manner in which these syndrome bits may be generated. More particularly, syndrome bit SI may be generated by XORing the received binary values in PI , D4, D3, and D 1. If none of the received data bits (D4, D3, Dl) is erroneous, the value of the received check bit PI is effectively XORed with itself, and the syndrome bit SI will be 0 (assuming the original check bit PI is not erroneous). If one of the data bits (D4, D3, Dl) or the check bit PI is erroneous, the syndrome bit SI will be 1 (asserted), thus indicating an error Syndrome bits S2 and S3 may be generated similarly. Taken collectively, the syndrome bits SI, S2 and S3 may be used to identify the location of an erroneous bit. For example, the binary value of the syndrome bits in the order [S3, S2, SI] indicates the position of the erroneous bit within the 7 bit data block as depicted in Figure 3. If the syndrome code is all zeros (i.e. "000"), the data has no smgle bit error. Upon identification of the erroneous bit position, the error is corrected by invertmg the binary value in that position, i.e. from 0 to 1 or from 1 to 0. It is a common practice to store data in, or communicate data through, multiple components. For example, a data block may be stored m a plurality of memory chips, or it may be communicated through a plurality of wires. An error may be introduced if one of the components is faulty. A Hamming code such as that descπbed above may be used to address error correction in such systems. For example, consider the case of storing D bits of data that are protected by C check bits using M memory chips. The data block therefore contains D+C bits. If the data block is to be evenly divided among the M memory chips, each memory chip will store X of the data and/or check bits of the data block, where X = (D+C)/M. The standard approach to providing error correction for chip failures is to divide the D+C data and check bits mto X logical groups each including M bits, and assigning 1 bit from each chip to each of the groups The check bits in each group form a SEC (single-error correcting) code such as a Hamming code. When any chip fails, it introduces at most one error into each group, and these errors are corrected independently us g the SEC codes. If a Hamming code is used m each group, a total of C = X*L check bits are required, where L is the smallest mteger such that 2ΛL > M This standard approach is inefficient because each group is able to independently identify which bit (if any) withm the group is in error However, if the only failures considered are memory chip failures, the failures in different groups are highly correlated.

It would be desirable to provide a system and method which allow for the reliable storage or transmission of data in environments wherem component failures are possible In particular, it would be desirable to provide a system and method which allows errors in data to be detected and corrected while reducmg the number of check bits which must be transmitted or stored.
SUMMARY OF THE INVENTION

The problems outlmed above may in large part be solved by a system and method for detectmg and correcting errors in a data block in accordance with the present mvention In one embodiment, a check bits generation unit receives and encodes data to be protected The check bits generation unit effectively partitions the data mto a plurality of logical groups The check bits generation unit generates a parity bit for each of the logical groups, and additionally generates a global error correction

The global error correction code is indicative of a predetermined combmation of a set of error correction codes each mdividually associated with a corresponding logical group In various embodiments, the global error correction code is equivalent to the result of generating individual error correction codes for each logical group and combmmg them in a predetermined manner

In one particular embodiment, the data is divided into a total of X logical groups The global error correction code may be equivalent to the result of (or may be derived by) shiftmg (either linearly or cyclically) the error correction code for a given ith group by l bit positions, wherein I = 0 to X-l, and by XORing corresponding columns of the resulting shifted error correction codes together The global error correction code, which in this case is referred to as having "twisted check" bits (by virtue of the selective shiftmg of the individual error correction codes), thus includes a separate bit indicating the parity for each aligned column formed by the collection of resulting shifted error correction codes The data along with the parity bit for each logical group and the global error correction code are then conveyed through a communication channel or are stored in memory Advantageously, the overall number of required check bits (the parity bits for the logical groups and the bits forming the global error correction code) is smaller than the overall number of bits needed for the collection of error correction codes associated mdividually with the logical groups In one implementation, data at corresponding bit positions withm the logical groups are conveyed through a common component, such as the same wire, or are stored in the same component, such as the same memory chip Additionally, data bits at different bit positions withm a given logical group are not conveyed through, or are not stored withm, a common component

An error correction unit is coupled to receive the plurality of data bits and the check bits following storage or transmission. The error correction unit is configured to generate a parity error bit for each of the logical groups of data based on the received data bits The error correction unit may further be configured to generate a regenerated global error correction code m the same manner in which the oπgmal global error correction code is deπved Thus, m one embodiment, the regenerated global error correction code is equivalent to the result of (or may be deπved by) shifting the regenerated error correction code for a given ith group by I bit positions, wherem l = 0 to X-l, and by XORing corresponding columns of the resultmg shifted error correction codes together A global syndrome code may be generated by XORing the oπgmal global error correction code with the regenerated global error correction code This global syndrome code is indicative of a difference between the original global error correction code and the regenerated global error correction code

In general, the global syndrome code is generated such that, with knowledge of the specific logical groups that have a single bit error, a value indicative of the location of the error m such groups may be denved
from the global syndrome code. The overall number of bits forming the global syndrome code and the parity bits for each logical group is smaller than the overall number of bits needed for the error correction codes mdividually associated with the logical groups.

In embodiments m which the error correction codes for various logical groups are shifted and XORed, the global syndrome code includes a bit corresponding to each aligned column of the regenerated shifted error correction codes which indicates whether a parity error for that column exists. The existence of a single bit error in any logical group can be determined using the oπgmal paπty bit and the data received for that group Additionally, smce the class of coπectable eπors considered by the system is restricted to single bit eπors that occur at the same position within the various logical groups (such errors may occur due to single component failures), the error coπection code for each logical group that has an eπor will reflect a change at exactly the same bit positions. Thus, by shifting the various eπor coπection codes m a twisted manner (i.e., shiftmg some more than others), and XORing the resulting vertically aligned columns, the coπelation that exists with respect to the specific bits that change in each error coπection code for each logic group with an eπor (l e., the eπor coπection code for each logical group having an eπor will mcur a change at exactly the same bit positions) may be exploited to thereby extract information indicating the specific bit position of the eπors
BRIEF DESCRIPTION OF THE DRAWINGS

Other objects and advantages of the invention will become apparent upon reading the following detailed descnption and upon reference to the accompanying drawings in which: Figure 1 (pnor art) is a block diagram illustrating a panty generator to encode data bits usmg a smgle eπor coπecting Hamming code;

While the mvention is susceptible to various modifications and alternative forms, specific embodiments thereof are shown by way of example m the drawings and will herein be descnbed in detail. It should be understood, however, that the drawings and detailed descnption thereto are not intended to limit the invention to the particular form disclosed, but on the contrary, the intention is to cover all modifications, equivalents and alternatives falling within the spirit and scope of the present invention as defined by the appended claims.
DETAILED DESCRIPTION OF THE DRAWINGS

Turning now to Figure 5, a block diagram of a system including an eπor control unit 105 is shown accordmg to one embodiment of the present invention. In this particular embodiment, the eπor control unit 105 is coupled to convey and receive data from storage 110. The storage 110 is configured to store a data block (data bits and check bits) that is communicated from/to the eπor control unit 105. The storage 110 mcludes a plurality of memory chips 1 lOA-110M. Each of the memory chips 1 lOA-110M is configured to store a portion of the data block. The memory chips 1 lOA-110M may be any type memory/ storage devices usable to store data.

As will be descπbed in further detail below, eπor control unit 105 is configured to encode data to be stored in the storage 110, and to decode received encoded data following storage to coπect certain categoπes of bit eπors (when they occur) usmg a relatively small number of check bits as compared with traditional approaches, such as typical single eπor coπecting Hamming codes.

The eπor control unit 105 includes a check bits generation unit 120 to perform the encoding process and an eπor coπection unit 130 to perform the decoding process and to perform eπor coπection. Data bits are received via data path 151 and are encoded by check bits generation unit 120 pnor to storing a data block (data bits and check bits) mto storage 110 via data path 152. Subsequently, the stored data block may be retneved by eπor coπection unit 130 via data path 153. Eπor coπection unit 130 decodes the data block to detect and coπect eπors in the data. If one or more eπors are detected, the eπors are coπected. The data bits (coπected, if necessary) are then output via data path 155
It is noted that check bits generation unit 120 and eπor coπection unit 130 may be implemented m hardware, in software, or using a combination thereof. Vanous specific implementations are possible.
The operation of eπor control unit 105 will next be explained with reference to Figures 5-8 Figures 6A-8B illustrate an example wherem a total of 20 data bits to be stored m storage 110 are protected

Figures 6A and 6B illustrate an encodmg process performed by the check bits generation unit 120 pnor to the storage of the data bits. Check bits generation unit 120 receives the 20 data bits (via data path 151) and,
in this example, processes the data accordmg to five logical groups, each group forming a respective row RO - R4, as shown in Figure 6A. A set of columns denoted D4, D3, D2, and Dl is formed by coπespondmg bit positions of each row. As will be descnbed m further detail below, the data forming each column is stored m the same memory chip, and different bits of each row are stored m different memory chips. Check bits generation unit 120 is configured to generate a panty bit per row (PPR) and a global eπor coπection code (GECC). The global eπor coπection code is equivalent to, or may be denved from a predetermined logical combmation of eπor coπection codes each mdividually associated with a respective row The PPR and GECC bits are check bits employed to protect the data bits against at most one eπor per row, provided that all eπors occur in the same column. The set of parity bits may be calculated usmg either even or odd parity. Since one parity bit is calculated per row, or logical group, the number of PPR bits equals the number of rows. In the example of Figure 6A, even panty is used. Thus, for the exemplary data as illustrated, each of the panty bits (PPRs) for rows R0-R3 is 1. The panty bit for row R4 is 0.

Figure 6A illustrates an eπor coπection code (ECC) associated with each row. In the example of Figure 6A, the eπor coπection code for each row is calculated accordmg to the assignment table shown in Figure 2. For example, the eπor coπection code calculated for the data m row R0 is [111], and the eπor coπection code calculated for row Rl is [011], and so on. It is noted, however, that other specific eπor coπection codmg techniques may be employed, and that different eπor coπection coding techniques may be associated with differing rows. Figure 6B illustrates a manner in which the global eπor coπection code may be generated. More particularly, in this embodiment, the global eπor coπection code may be generated by selectively shiftmg certain row ECCs with respect to one another and XORing the resulting vertically aligned bits. Smce some of the row ECCs are shifted more than others, the bits forming the global eπor coπection code are refeπed to as "twisted" check bits. In the embodiment of Figure 6B, the global eπor coπection code is denved by linearly shiftmg the eπor coπection code for a given ith group by l bit positions wherein l = 0 to X-l, and where X is the total number of rows or logical groups The bits in each resultmg vertically aligned column are then XORed together, to thereby generate the global eπor coπection code (leadmg or trailing 0s may be added to the entπes of each row of the twisted ECCs, as necessary, pnor to this XOR operation).

It is noted that m the discussion above relatmg to Figures 6A and 6B, the global eπor coπection code is calculated by first generating the mdividual eπor coπection codes for each row and logically combming them in a predetermined manner. In other embodiments, the global eπor coπection code may be generated directly from the data bits such that it is equivalent to the result of generating individual eπor coπection codes for each row and combming them m a predetermined manner For example, the global eπor coπection code illustrated in Figure 6B could be generated directly from the data bits using a predetermined function, without generatmg individual eπor coπection codes for each row

Upon calculation of the global eπor coπection code, the data block mcludmg 20 bits of data, the panty bits (PPRs) and the global eπor coπection code (GECC) are conveyed to storage 110. It is noted that the bits forming each column (D4, D3, D2, and Dl) of data m the data block are stored m a common memory chip, and that no two data bits in differing bit positions of a particular row are stored m the same memory chip. It is
further noted that the panty bits and global eπor coπection code (GECC) may be stored m additional memory chips. A further example of the manner in which the panty bits and the bits forming the global eπor coπection code (GECC) may be distnbuted for storage within vanous memory chips will be provided further below m conjunction with Figures 20-35 It is further noted that in the example of Figures 6 A and 6B, a total of 12 check bits (the panty bits

(PPRs) and the bits of the global ECC) are generated for storage along with the 20 data bits This overall number of check bits is advantageously less than the number of check bits required usmg conventional methods (wherem, for example, a total of 15 check bits, coπesponding to the row eπor coπection codes, are necessary) Generally speaking, m embodiments which employ a linearly shifted global eπor coπection code generated accordmg to the example of Figure 6B, a total of only (2X+L-1) check bits are needed, where it is assumed that D bits of data are protected with C check bits using M memory chips (where M evenly divides (D+C)), and where X=(D+C)/M and C=X*L where L is the smallest mteger such that 2ΛL≥M

Referring now to Figures 7A - 8B, the decodmg process of the data block following storage will next be explained. As illustrated in Figure 7A, eπor coπection unit 130 processes the data accordmg to the same logical groups as formed by check bits generation unit 120 Eπor coπection unit 130 may be configured to generate a regenerated parity bit per row (PPR') using the received data The same parity type (even or odd) is used duπng both encoding and decoding In the example of Figure 7A, two eπors are introduced mto the received data set, both occurring m column D2, as shown with underlmes More particularly, the bits m rows Rl and R3 of column D2 have been changed to exemplify eπors. Such eπors could be the result of, for example, a faulty memory chip that stores the column D2 bits of the data set. Thus, for this example, the regenerated panty bits for rows Rl and R3 change state. A bit for each row indicating that a panty eπor exists may be generated by XOR g the ongmal parity bits with the regenerated panty bits. It is noted that generation of these row panty eπor bits (RPEs) may instead be generated directly by XORmg coπespondmg bits of the received data bits with the ongmal panty bits (PPRs) (without separately generating the regenerated panty bits (PPRs))

If any of the rows have a single bit eπor, as indicated by the row panty eπor bits (RPEs), the eπor coπection unit 130 generates a regenerated global eπor coπection code in the same manner m which the ongmal global eπor coπection code was generated, usmg the regenerated eπor coπection codes. Thus, in one embodiment, the regenerated global eπor coπection code may be denved by shiftmg the eπor coπection code for a given ith group by I bit positions, where I = 0 - X-l, and by XORmg the bits m the resulting vertically aligned columns, as depicted m Figure 7B Similar to the previous discussion, in other embodiments, the regenerated global eπor coπection code may be denved directly from a predetermined function of the received data bits, without generating an mdividual eπor coπection code for each row In such embodiments, however, the global eπor coπection code is equivalent to a predetermined combmation of a set of eπor coπection codes each individually associated with a coπespondmg row

As shown m Figure 8 A, upon generation of the regenerated global eπor coπection code, a global syndrome code may be generated by XORing the ongmal global eπor coπection code with the regenerated global eπor coπection code. This global syndrome code is indicative of a difference between the oπgmal global eπor coπection code and the regenerated global eπor coπection code. In embodiments m which the
eπor coπection codes for various logical groups are effectively shifted in a twisted manner and are XORed, the global syndrome code mcludes a bit coπespondmg to each aligned column of the regenerated shifted eπor coπection codes which indicates whether a paπty eπor for that column exists. For mstance, m the example of Figure 8, the bits m the global syndrome code for positions 2, 3, 4 and 5 are set This is the result of the fact that the parity in each of columns 2, 3, 4 and 5 of the shifted regenerated eπor coπection codes of Figure 7B is different from the parity of each of the coπesponding columns of the original shifted eπor coπection codes, as depicted in Figure 6B Accordingly, in this embodiment the global syndrome code includes a bit coπespondmg to each aligned column of the regenerated shifted eπor coπection codes which indicates whether a paπty eπor for that column exists. Since the regenerated eπor coπection codes for the logical groups that have eπors will incur changes at exactly the same bit positions, by shifting in a twisted manner the various eπor coπection codes and XORing the resulting bit aligned columns, the coπelation that exists with respect to changes m the eπor coπection codes for logical groups that have eπors may be exploited to thereby extract information indicating the specific positions of the eπors.

For example, Figure 8B illustrates a manner m which a set of row syndrome codes, each of which is indicative of the position of an eπor in a given row, may be generated using the global syndrome code and the row panty eπor information. As illustrated in Figure 8B, entries (initially unfilled) for each row syndrome code are provided by shifting the entries in the same manner m which the eπor coπection codes were shifted to generate the global eπor coπection code. First, the row syndrome codes for any rows that do not have eπors can be filled in with all "0" values (since rows without eπors could not contnbute to a parity eπor m any given column, as identified by the global syndrome code). Thus, the row syndrome code entries for rows R0, R2, and R4 can be filled in with all "0" values. As depicted in Figure 8B, the first row with an eπor is row Rl. Smce the first bit of the row syndrome code for row Rl is in column position 1, and smce the global syndrome value for that bit position is 0 and the only other contnbuting value for that bit position of the global syndrome code is denved from the row syndrome code for row R0 (which is already known to be "0"), the value of the first bit of the row syndrome code for row Rl can be filled in as "0" Additionally, since the row syndrome code for every row with an eπor is known to be identical, the first bit of the row syndrome code for row R3 can also be filled in as a "0". Subsequently, the second bit of the syndrome code for row Rl may be similarly determined by considering the value in bit position 2 of the global syndrome, and the values of the bits m position 2 of rows 0 and 2 (I e., the last bit of the row syndrome code for row R0 and the first bit of the row syndrome code for row R2). In this situation, the value of the second bit of the row syndrome code for row Rl may be filled in as a "1". Again, this value is also reflected m the second bit of the row syndrome code for row R3. The last bit of the row syndrome codes may be determined similarly

The binary value of the row syndrome codes (taken in reverse order with respect to the depicted values m Figure 8B) thus indicates the position of the eπor for logical groups that have eπors Therefore, in this example, the value "110", which is binary 6, coπelates to bit position D2, as shown in Figure 3. This position coπesponds to the position of the eπors introduced m the example shown in Figure 7A.

Upon determination of the eπoneous bits m the received data set, the eπor coπection unit 230 is configured to coπect the data, as needed. For example, m the example of Figures 6-8, the bits m column D2 of
the rows Rl and R3 are identified as bemg eπoneous Accordingly, eπor coπection unit 230 inverts these bits and outputs the data as coπected via data output 155

Turning next to Figures 9-17, a manner in which the row panty information and the global syndrome information may be decoded to generate the row syndrome code is next considered More particularly, as illustrated m Figure 9, eπor coπection unit 130 may employ an RPE/global syndrome code generation unit 131 and a linear shift unit 132 for decoding a received data block which is encoded usmg the linear shiftmg methodology as described above A functional block diagram illustrating functional aspects of the linear shift unit 132 is illustrated m Figure 10 As shown, lmear shift unit 132 includes a control unit 135 coupled to a pair of shift registers 133 and 134 The various functionality illustrated in Figures 9 and 10 may be implemented m hardware, m software, or usmg a combination thereof

The RPE/global syndrome code generation unit 131 generates the row parity eπor bits (RPEs) and the global syndrome code m accordance with the foregomg description using the received data block The row panty eπor bits (RPEs) and the global syndrome code are then provided to the lmear shift unit 132
